why: Comparing drops on grass tips, a half-wet bench and frost helps your child use evidence to explain where morning water really comes from.
teaser: Find drops on every grass tip, then meet water a plant pushes out, a bench that is only half wet, feathers of ice and a glow around your shadow.
title: The Secret Life of Morning Dew
question: Where do the morning's drops really come from?
idea: Dew is not rain. It grows on things that get cold under a clear night sky, when water hiding in the air turns into drops, or into frost if it is freezing. Some drops on leaf tips are not dew at all: the plant pushed them out from its roots.

curiosity.intro: Start with a drop on every grass tip. Then meet water from inside a plant, a half-wet bench, feathers of ice and a desert beetle that drinks fog.
curiosity.carryForward: Next clear, still morning, look for drops on grass tips and check which things stayed dry.

questions.question: Can a plant make its own drops?
questions.notice: Find a drop on the tip of each little tooth around the leaf, while the middle of the leaf stays dry.
questions.say: Yes! At night, when the soil is damp, the roots keep pushing water up into the leaves. The extra water squeezes out of tiny holes at the leaf tips and edges. This is called guttation. Those drops look like dew, but they came from inside the plant.
questions.try: Water a small potted plant well in the evening. Set a clear bowl upside down over it for the night. In the morning, look at the leaf tips and edges. Are the drops all over, or lined up at the tips?

questions.question: Why is only half of the bench wet?
questions.notice: Compare the beaded, open half of the bench with the dry half under the branch.
questions.say: All night, things give their warmth away to the clear sky and grow cold. The open half got cold enough for water in the air to turn into drops on it. The branch sent some warmth back down, like a blanket, so that half stayed dry. Clouds and wind can stop dew too.
questions.try: Fill one glass with ice water and one glass with tap water. Wait five minutes. Which glass grows drops on the outside? Wipe it dry and watch the drops come back.

questions.question: Where do frost feathers come from?
questions.notice: Find the white ice feathers growing out from the leaf edge and veins. Are there any round drops?
questions.say: On a freezing night, the leaf gets colder than ice. Then the water hiding in the air skips the drop step. It turns straight into ice crystals, called frost. The crystals keep growing outward, so they look like tiny white feathers.
questions.try: Fill a clean metal can with ice and stir in two big spoons of salt. Wait about ten minutes. Look for white frost growing on the outside of the can.

questions.question: How can a beetle drink fog?
questions.notice: Find the beetle's raised back end, its bumpy black back and the drop rolling toward its head.
questions.say: In a foggy desert by the sea, it almost never rains. At dawn, this beetle climbs a dune and tips its back up into the fog. Tiny fog drops stick to its bumpy back, join into bigger drops and roll down to its mouth. People copy this trick with big nets that catch fog water.
questions.try: Drip water onto wax paper and onto a paper towel. Tilt both pieces. Where do the drops roll like beads, and where do they soak in?

plates.title: A drop on every tip
plates.alt: At dawn beside a dry stone garden path, Little Wonderer kneels at the edge of tall grass, one mitten raised near the blades, while Big Wonderer leans in behind. Many grass blades hold small round clear drops, several right at their tips.
plates.caption: The path is dry, yet the grass is beaded with drops. No rain fell, so where did this water come from?

plates.title: Drops from inside
plates.alt: A three-part strawberry leaf on pale paper. The leaf surface is dry, but a small round clear drop sits on the tip of every little tooth around its edge, like a necklace.
plates.caption: Guttation: the roots pushed this water up and out of tiny holes at the tooth tips. These drops came from inside the plant.

plates.title: Half a wet bench
plates.alt: A wooden garden bench on a dewy lawn at dawn. The left half of the seat and armrest, open to the sky, is covered in tiny clear beads; the right half, under a leafy tree branch, is in shade and dry, and the grass there has no drops.
plates.caption: The open half lost its warmth to the clear sky and grew dew. The branch sent warmth back, so the sheltered half stayed dry.

plates.title: Feathers of ice
plates.alt: A fallen green-and-brown leaf on frosty ground, its edges and veins furred with fine white feathery ice crystals, beside grass blades fringed with frost.
plates.caption: On a freezing night, water from the air turned straight into ice crystals. Frost grows outward like feathers; it never fell.

plates.title: A glow around a shadow
plates.alt: On a dewy lawn at sunrise, Little Wonderer stands and points at two long shadows stretching across the wet grass, while Big Wonderer sits close beside. A soft pale glow brightens the grass around the head of each shadow.
plates.caption: Dew drops bounce sunlight back toward the sun, so the wet grass glows around a shadow's head. In real life, each looker sees the glow only around its own shadow.

plates.title: A beetle drinks fog
plates.alt: A black bumpy-backed darkling beetle stands head-down on a pale sand dune at dawn, with fog drifting in from the sea behind it. Clear drops sit on the bumps of its back, and one larger drop has rolled near its head.
plates.caption: In a foggy desert, this beetle tips its back into the fog. Drops gather on the bumps and roll down to its mouth.

poem.title: The Dew Watch
lines: Little Wonderer said, “I will catch the dew fall!”
So out went a jar and a stool by the wall.
“It drips from the stars every night,” came the cry,
“and I’ll catch every drop as it falls from the sky!”
Big Wonderer smiled and left on the porch light.
The little one stared at the stars half the night.
But the sky never dripped, not a drop, not a pour,
and the little one nodded and drifted to snore.
At dawn, the grass glittered. The jar was wet too,
but the drops were OUTSIDE it, a jacket of dew!
“How did they get on it, if none of them fell?”
asked the little one, peeking inside the dry shell.
“It never fell down,” said the big one. “It grew,
when the air touched the cold glass and gave it some dew.”
So now every night there’s a jar by the wall,
upside down, catching dew that won’t ever fall.
